A systematic review was conducted to evaluate treatment options for chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, focusing on direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) for genotypes 1 through 6. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized comparative trials, single-arm trials, and observational studies. The primary outcomes assessed were sustained virologic response at 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12), discontinuations due to adverse events (DAEs), serious adverse events (SAEs), and mortality. Evidence was stratified by HCV genotype, treatment experience (treatment-naïve or treatment-experienced), and patient subgroups (e.g., those with cirrhosis or HCV/HIV co-infection). The systematic search spanned three major medical literature databases (EMBASE, MEDLINE, and CENTRAL) and recent conference proceedings. The review period covered publications from January 1, 2015, onward. A previously commissioned systematic review was also cross-referenced to identify updated outcome data. Evidence synthesis involved pooling untransformed proportions of SVR12, DAEs, SAEs, and mortality for each treatment and population stratification, generating point estimates with 95% confidence intervals. The findings demonstrated high SVR12 rates across most treatments and patient stratifications, although evidence for patients with genotypes 2 or 3 and cirrhosis was mixed. Limited evidence was available for patients with HCV/HIV co-infection, but SVR12 rates were generally high. Safety outcomes, including DAEs, SAEs, and mortality, were consistently low across all treatments and genotypes. The review emphasized that inferences on relative treatment effects should be avoided due to the non-comparative analytical approach. The objective was to synthesize evidence on the efficacy and safety of antiviral therapies for chronic HCV infection, specifically focusing on SVR12 rates and safety outcomes such as DAEs, SAEs, and mortality. Eligibility criteria excluded retrospective studies, study arms with fewer than 20 patients (except for pan-genotypic regimens), and studies where outcomes were not stratified by intervention. Data extraction and quality assessments were conducted independently by multiple investigators, with discrepancies resolved through discussion or arbitration. Analyses were performed using OpenMeta[Analyst] software, and results were stratified by treatment experience and patient subgroups. In conclusion, the systematic review highlighted the efficacy of DAAs in achieving high SVR12 rates across most patient populations, with some variability in outcomes for specific genotypes and subgroups. Safety outcomes were favorable, with low rates of adverse events and mortality.
